verdicts.text: SST moved from AWS CDK to Pulumi, unlocking multi-cloud flexibility, faster deployments, and a better developer experience; Pulumi offers a more flexible, provider-agnostic approach to infrastructure management.
verdicts.evidence: SST's own post confirms Ion drops CDK: "The constructs (or components) are defined using Terraform providers and deployed using Pulumi; as opposed to CDK and CloudFormation (CFN)." It also says the team watched "all the CDK issues we listed basically vanish." The multi-cloud, speed and developer-experience benefits are the blog's own summary of SST's reasoning. SST's post does back that summary: it moves away from the CloudFormation "black box" and uses Terraform providers, which aren't tied to one cloud.
verdicts.framing_note: The core fact (SST moved from CDK to Pulumi) matches SST's post exactly. The benefits ("multi-cloud flexibility, faster deployments, better DX") are the blog's own summary. SST's post supports them in spirit but doesn't list them as a set.
verdicts.intuition_flag: "Faster deployments" and "multi-cloud" are the blog's paraphrase and aren't quoted as SST's stated reasons. A reviewer may want to tie them to specific lines in SST's post.

verdicts.text: Debugging AWS CDK is frustrating because CDK generates CloudFormation templates (an intermediary YAML/JSON format) that are then executed, so the code you write is not the code that runs during deployment.
verdicts.evidence: AWS CDK docs confirm the mechanism: cdk synth produces "a cloud assembly, including an AWS CloudFormation template for each stack", and CloudFormation then deploys that template. The claim is attributed to SST in the post, and "frustrating" is an opinion that can't be checked. The checkable part, that CDK code is compiled into CloudFormation templates and CloudFormation runs those templates rather than your code, is accurate.
verdicts.framing_note: The AWS docs describe CDK turning code into CloudFormation templates. The claim adds a subjective point about debugging that no source can confirm or refute.

verdicts.text: Multi-cloud deployment was nearly impossible with AWS CDK.
verdicts.evidence: SST's docs describe v3 as leaving CloudFormation and CDK behind, and say its new Pulumi providers let users "build on any cloud". That implies the CDK-based v2 had no real multi-cloud path. Because AWS CDK deploys through CloudFormation, it is essentially AWS-only, so the claim holds as a description. "Nearly impossible" is the blog's own editorial wording, not a direct quote from SST.
verdicts.framing_note: The claim reads as the blog's own summary of CDK's limits, not a quote from SST. SST's original post focuses on CDK/CloudFormation design flaws such as slowness and rollbacks. The multi-cloud benefit is described as "150+ other providers that allow you to build on any cloud."
verdicts.intuition_flag: "Nearly impossible" is hyperbole: CDK custom resources and CDKTF (which was multi-cloud and is now deprecated) existed. Still, the core point that AWS CDK is AWS-only is accurate.

verdicts.text: The table-of-contents links use the alias path /blog/from-cdk-pulumi-evolution-of-sst/ with anchors matching the post's section headings (e.g., #the-beginnings-of-sst).
verdicts.evidence: The front matter lists `aliases: - /blog/from-cdk-pulumi-evolution-of-sst/`. All six TOC links on L76-81 point to that path, and each anchor matches the slug of an H2 heading in the post: "The Beginnings of SST" (L83), "CDK and CloudFormation Limitations" (L89), "A Provider-agnostic Solution: Discovering Pulumi" (L110), "Transitioning to Pulumi" (L120), "The Benefits of Pulumi" (L128) and "The Future of SST with Pulumi" (L162).
verdicts.source: repo:content/blog/aws-cdk-vs-pulumi-why-sst-switched/index.md (L59-60 aliases, L76-81 TOC, H2 headings at L83-L162)
verdicts.intuition_flag: The anchors work only if the alias redirect keeps the fragment. Links to the post's own path, or relative `#anchor` links, would be more robust.

verdicts.text: SST was originally built on top of AWS's Cloud Development Kit (CDK), which allowed developers to define infrastructure using TypeScript or Python.
verdicts.evidence: SST's own blog confirms the CDK foundation: "At the end of the day, SST v2 is open source and built on CDK." A secondary source adds that "the first two versions of SST were basically the wrappers and enhancers of AWS CDK." The language clause is about CDK, which does support TypeScript and Python (plus Java, C# and Go), but that comes from general knowledge, not from these results.
verdicts.framing_note: SST source says "SST v2 ... built on CDK"; the claim says "SST was originally built on top of AWS's CDK", which is the same assertion.
verdicts.intuition_flag: "TypeScript or Python" is correct for CDK, but readers may take it to mean SST itself let you define infrastructure in Python. SST infrastructure code was TypeScript/JavaScript only, and CDK also supports Java, C# and Go.

verdicts.text: AWS CDK allows developers to define their infrastructure using TypeScript or Python.
verdicts.evidence: The official AWS CDK guide says CDK "has first-class support for the TypeScript, JavaScript, Python, Java, C#, and Go general-purpose programming languages." That confirms TypeScript and Python are both supported. They are not the only languages, but the claim doesn't say they are.
verdicts.framing_note: The source lists six supported languages. The claim names two of them (TypeScript, Python), which the source covers as a special case.
verdicts.intuition_flag: "TypeScript or Python" could read as a complete list. CDK also supports JavaScript, Java, C#, and Go, so the author might want to add "among others."

verdicts.text: With AWS CDK and CloudFormation, the infrastructure code is essentially a code generator that produces an intermediary format (such as YAML or JSON) which is then executed to deploy the resources.
verdicts.evidence: The AWS CDK docs describe synthesis as "the process of producing an AWS CloudFormation template and deployment artifacts from a CDK stack", and "The cloud assembly is what gets deployed to provision your resources on AWS." The cdk synth reference says the template goes to stdout "in YAML format". So the claim is correct: CDK code works like a code generator that outputs an intermediate CloudFormation template (JSON/YAML), and that template is what gets deployed.
verdicts.framing_note: The claim's "code generator" wording is the author's own description, but the AWS docs' account of synthesis (CDK code produces a CloudFormation template, which is then deployed) supports it.

verdicts.text: With AWS CDK, the code a developer writes is not the same as the code running during the deployment process, leading to difficulty debugging, lack of visibility into the deployment process, and challenges extending or customizing the deployment workflow.
verdicts.evidence: The factual core holds up. Pulumi's CDK comparison page says CDK is a transpiler whose programs "are synthesized into CloudFormation templates" that the CloudFormation service deploys, so the code you write isn't what runs during deployment. The listed downsides (harder debugging, less visibility, harder to extend) are the SST team's view as reported in the post, not measurable facts.
verdicts.framing_note: Mechanism corroborated by a same-site comparison page. The consequences are a subjective judgment credited to SST, not an independently checkable fact.

verdicts.text: The Pulumi docs page at https://www.pulumi.com/docs/iac/comparisons/cloudformation/ has a section 'what-is-aws-cloudformation'.
verdicts.evidence: The comparison page has the heading "## What is AWS CloudFormation?" on L37. Hugo turns that heading into the anchor #what-is-aws-cloudformation, so the link target exists.
verdicts.framing_note: The heading "What is AWS CloudFormation?" becomes the anchor what-is-aws-cloudformation.

verdicts.text: The Pulumi docs page at /docs/iac/comparisons/aws-cdk/ has a section (anchor #what-is-aws-cdk) describing the AWS-centric nature of CDK; the CloudFormation comparison page has an anchor #what-is-aws-cloudformation.
verdicts.evidence: Both anchors exist in the repo. aws-cdk.md L35 has "## What is AWS CDK?" and says "CDK is AWS-only." cloudformation.md L37 has "## What is AWS CloudFormation?"

verdicts.text: Pulumi supports multi-cloud deployment across AWS, Azure, GCP, and on-premises.
verdicts.evidence: A third-party MinIO blog says that with Pulumi, users can deploy "to their private cloud, Azure, Google Cloud, AWS as well as a rich ecosystem of bare metal providers", and later adds that you can "even manage resources on-premises". Pulumi's own Why Pulumi page says the same thing ("AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, Kubernetes, and hybrid/on-prem"), and a 2020 BusinessWire release names public, private and hybrid cloud providers.
verdicts.framing_note: Sources name AWS, Azure, Google Cloud and hybrid/on-prem, which matches the claim's list.

verdicts.text: AWS CDK supports only TypeScript and Python as programming languages (the table marks CDK language support as limited to TypeScript, Python).
verdicts.evidence: The official AWS CDK v2 guide says CDK "has first-class support for the TypeScript, JavaScript, Python, Java, C#, and Go general-purpose programming languages." So the table's "TypeScript, Python" leaves out four officially supported languages. Those two were only the launch languages at GA in 2019.
verdicts.intuition_flag: The table may be mixing up CDK with SST's own language support, or using the GA-era (2019) language list.

verdicts.text: Pulumi supports any programming language.
verdicts.evidence: Pulumi's docs list a fixed set of supported languages: "Pulumi supports many of today's most common general-purpose programming and markup languages" (TypeScript/JS, Python, Go, .NET, Java, YAML, HCL), and note separately that "it is possible to add your own language." The "any programming language" wording is Pulumi's marketing tagline (the GitHub repo title), not a literal capability.
verdicts.framing_note: overclaim — docs say "supports many of today's most common ... languages"; claim says "supports any programming language"
verdicts.intuition_flag: "Any" is absolute; consider "multiple general-purpose languages (TypeScript, Python, Go, C#, Java, YAML)".

verdicts.text: Pulumi treats infrastructure code as a first-class program executed directly during deployment rather than generating an intermediary format; the infrastructure code is the same code that runs during deployment.
verdicts.evidence: Pulumi's architecture docs say "Programs are executed by a language host process, which wraps the runtime for a given language in an interface that the deployment engine can interact with". The program registers resources with the engine over gRPC during `pulumi up`, and no template (like CloudFormation's) is synthesized first. The "rather than an intermediary format" part is inferred from this architecture; the docs don't say it word for word.
verdicts.framing_note: Source: the language host executes the program and resource registrations go straight to the engine. Claim: the code runs directly during deployment, with no intermediary format. The contrast with an intermediary format is implied by the architecture, not stated.

verdicts.text: With Pulumi, the infrastructure code is the same code that runs during deployment, giving greater visibility into the deployment process and the ability to extend or customize it.
verdicts.evidence: Pulumi's developer architecture docs, which live in the pulumi/pulumi repo, say "As a Pulumi program is executed by the language host, it will make RegisterResource calls to the engine." That supports the claim's main point: the user's infrastructure code runs during the deployment itself, not as a template generator the way CDK→CloudFormation is. The "greater visibility" and "extend/customize" parts are subjective benefits that follow from this design. They aren't independently measurable, and SST's own post doesn't state them in these words.
verdicts.framing_note: Architecture docs: 'program is executed by the language host... RegisterResource calls to the engine' → claim: 'infrastructure code is the same code that runs during deployment'; the benefits clause is the author's own qualitative framing.
verdicts.intuition_flag: The second half (visibility, extensibility) is a marketing-style benefit, not something you can check.

verdicts.text: Pulumi's provider-agnostic approach allowed SST's team to easily add support for new cloud and on-premises providers, and SST users can manage all their infrastructure through a single, consistent interface without juggling multiple tools.
verdicts.evidence: SST's own announcement confirms it adopted "the Pulumi deployment engine and their bridged Terraform providers" and says there is "nothing else to install", but it never says Pulumi let the team "easily add" cloud/on-prem providers or gave users "a single, consistent interface without juggling multiple tools". The only source with that wording is the reviewed Pulumi blog itself, and a page can't count as proof of its own claims.
verdicts.framing_note: SST source: "Pulumi deployment engine and their bridged Terraform providers" (no stated multi-cloud/on-prem ease or single-interface benefit). The claim credits SST with benefits the SST source doesn't state.
verdicts.intuition_flag: 'On-premises providers' and 'without juggling multiple tools' read as Pulumi marketing attributed to SST; SST's own post focuses on escaping CloudFormation/CDK issues, not multi-cloud.

verdicts.text: The SST team's migration from CDK to Pulumi required re-implementing the higher-level components and abstractions built on top of CDK and handling edge cases and complex deployment scenarios from the CDK-based version.
verdicts.evidence: SST's own post confirms that its components were rebuilt on Pulumi rather than CDK: "you cannot use a CDK construct in Ion. You'll need to migrate it over." The SST v2→v3 migration doc adds that apps using higher-level CDK constructs are "really hard to migrate." The specific "handling edge cases and complex deployment scenarios" part does not appear in the SST sources I found.
verdicts.framing_note: SST's sources support re-implementing the CDK-based components on Pulumi. The edge-cases/complex-deployment part is the author's reasonable reading, not something SST says.
verdicts.intuition_flag: The "edge cases and complex deployment scenarios" wording is generic and may be LLM-generated elaboration that SST never actually said.

verdicts.text: A Founding Engineer at SST said: "With Pulumi, the deployment process feels like a natural extension of writing code - it's intuitive and powerful and capable of advanced things that traditional IaC tools can't handle."
verdicts.evidence: Two searches turned up no independent source for this quote. The only relevant result is the live copy of the post under review, which can't verify itself. A separate result confirms that SST had a Founding Engineer: PulumiUP 2024 lists "Dax Raad (Founding Engineer, SST)" as a speaker on "From CDK to Pulumi: Evolution of SST". The quote may come from that talk, but I couldn't find a transcript.
verdicts.source: WebSearch ran query "\"deployment process feels like a natural extension of writing code\" Pulumi"; top results didn't address the claim. Corroborating context: https://www.pulumi.com/blog/pulumiup-global-cloud-iac-platform-engineering-ai-conference/
verdicts.framing_note: The quote is credited only to a role, not a named person, and I found no primary source such as a talk transcript or interview to compare the wording against.
verdicts.intuition_flag: The wording ("intuitive and powerful and capable of advanced things that traditional IaC tools can't handle") reads like a paraphrase or marketing copy rather than a spoken quote. The author should confirm it is verbatim and link the source, e.g. the PulumiUP 2024 talk.

verdicts.text: Pulumi Insights (https://www.pulumi.com/product/pulumi-insights/) provides improved visibility and debugging capabilities into deployments.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) Pulumi's own materials describe Insights as giving visibility into cloud infrastructure and resources through search, analytics, discovery and policy compliance. Pulumi's docs say "Pulumi Insights enables visibility into cloud resources and compliance monitoring." None of the sources found describe it as a tool for debugging deployments. The visibility part of the claim holds up; "debugging capabilities into deployments" does not.
verdicts.framing_note: shifted: the source says 'visibility into cloud resources and compliance monitoring'; the claim says 'visibility and debugging capabilities into deployments'. Deployment debugging (update logs, diffs) is a Pulumi Cloud/Deployments feature, not Insights.
verdicts.intuition_flag: The cited product page (/product/pulumi-insights/) did not come up directly in search results; it may have moved to the Insights & Governance pages.

verdicts.text: Pulumi has built-in extensibility features such as custom providers and dynamic components that SST leveraged to integrate with cloud and on-premises services and implement complex deployment workflows.
verdicts.evidence: Pulumi does have custom providers and dynamic providers ("lighter weight than custom providers"), and SST components are Pulumi ComponentResources. But the only source saying SST used "custom providers and dynamic components" for cloud/on-prem integrations is the reviewed blog post's own live copy. SST's own "Moving away from CDK" and v3 posts only describe bridged Terraform providers on an embedded Pulumi engine.
verdicts.source: https://www.pulumi.com/docs/iac/concepts/providers/dynamic-providers/; https://sst.dev/blog/moving-away-from-cdk/; https://sst.dev/blog/sst-v3/; WebSearch ran query "SST v3 Pulumi dynamic providers components why switched from CDK"
verdicts.intuition_flag: Pulumi has no feature called "dynamic components" (the terms are dynamic providers and component resources), and "on-premises services" doesn't fit SST's cloud/serverless focus. The sentence also slips into first person ("our users") in the live copy, so it may be paraphrased or generated rather than sourced from SST.

verdicts.text: With CDK/CloudFormation, SST often had to resort to hacky workarounds or custom Lambda functions to customize the deployment process.
verdicts.evidence: SST's own "Moving away from CDK" post says the CDK community "(and us included) need to rely on this for basically anything that isn't supported". Here "this" means Lambda-backed Custom Resources. The post also says "CloudFormation is a black box and CDK has to create these hacks to work around it."
verdicts.framing_note: SST's post says it relied on Custom Resources (Lambda functions) and hacks for anything CDK/CloudFormation doesn't support. That broader statement covers the claim's narrower "to customize the deployment process". The live Pulumi page is the reviewed file, so it was not used as evidence.

verdicts.text: With Pulumi, the SST team was able to easily add support for new providers.
verdicts.evidence: SST's own docs say it is "built on Pulumi/Terraform and supports 150+ providers," and a single `sst add` command adds a provider. SST's "Moving away from CDK" post adds that the team can "fork the provider if necessary and create our own," and SST publishes bridged providers such as sst/pulumi-supabase.
verdicts.framing_note: SST's sources describe broad provider support that Pulumi makes possible, plus the ability to fork or bridge providers. "Easily add support for new providers" is a fair but subjective paraphrase. No SST source uses the word "easily."

verdicts.text: With SST built on Pulumi, users can manage all of their infrastructure across multiple cloud providers and on-premises through a single, consistent interface.
verdicts.evidence: SST's docs back up the main point, that SST is built on Pulumi and works across multiple clouds: "SST is built on Pulumi/Terraform and supports 150+ providers. This includes the major clouds like AWS, Azure, and GCP". But no SST source says it manages "on-premises" infrastructure or "all of their infrastructure".
verdicts.framing_note: overclaim: the claim takes "supports 150+ providers... major clouds like AWS, Azure, and GCP" and stretches it to "all of their infrastructure across multiple cloud providers and on-premises"
verdicts.intuition_flag: "On-premises" looks like generic Pulumi marketing copy applied to SST, whose docs only talk about cloud and SaaS providers.

verdicts.text: Pulumi lets you define infrastructure in TypeScript, Python, Go, or C# and deploy it across AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, and on-premises environments from one consistent workflow.
verdicts.evidence: Pulumi docs say it "supports TypeScript, JavaScript, Python, Go, .NET, Java, YAML, and HCL." The IaC docs also say it can "Manage infrastructure across AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, Kubernetes, and thousands of cloud providers." So the claim's list of four languages is a correct subset, and C# runs on .NET. The on-premises part relies on the Kubernetes provider and other providers such as vSphere.
verdicts.framing_note: The claim names only 4 of the 8 supported languages ("or" doesn't claim the list is complete). The docs list cloud targets as AWS/Azure/GCP/Kubernetes and more; on-premises isn't named outright but is covered by those providers.

verdicts.text: The SST team is exploring deeper integration with application frameworks, expanded cloud and on-premises provider support, improved deployment workflows (faster deployment times, better rollback capabilities, more granular control), and enhanced observability and monitoring built on Pulumi.
verdicts.evidence: I couldn't find any independent SST source (sst.dev blog, SST team statement) for this roadmap. The only copy is the live Pulumi blog page under review (2024), which lists "Expanded Provider Support", "Improved Deployment Workflows" and "Enhanced Observability and Monitoring" as Pulumi's own description, not a quote from SST. Also, pulumi/docs PR #21673 calls this closing paragraph a "2024 speculative-roadmap" and says SST's team has since shifted focus to other projects (opencode).
verdicts.source: WebSearch ran query "SST roadmap Pulumi future plans observability rollback" and "SST blog Ion Pulumi future on-premises providers"; only https://www.pulumi.com/blog/aws-cdk-vs-pulumi-why-sst-switched/ (the reviewed page itself) and https://github.com/pulumi/docs/pull/21673 addressed it
verdicts.intuition_flag: This roadmap is attributed to the SST team in the present tense, but it reads like 2024 speculation by Pulumi and no SST source backs it. A later docs PR (#21673) replaces it as stale, and the "on-premises" providers and "observability built on Pulumi" items have no SST backing.

verdicts.text: The Pulumi Cloud Deployments docs (/docs/pulumi-cloud/deployments/) describe advanced deployment workflows.
verdicts.evidence: The /docs/pulumi-cloud/deployments/ link still works because it is an alias of content/docs/deployments/concepts/_index.md ("Pulumi Deployments"). That page covers running operations "on demand, in response to version control events, on a schedule, or through the REST API", which fits "advanced deployment workflows".
verdicts.framing_note: The link is a legacy alias. The canonical path is now /docs/deployments/concepts/, so the author could update the link to avoid a redirect.

verdicts.text: Pulumi Insights provides better visibility into the deployment process and more robust monitoring and observability.
verdicts.evidence: L169 is a roadmap bullet about what the SST team plans to build, not a statement about what Pulumi Insights can do: "they can provide their users with [better visibility](…/pulumi-insights/) into the deployment process and more robust monitoring and observability capabilities". The extracted claim rewrites that future goal as a Pulumi Insights feature, which the line never asserts.
verdicts.framing_note: shifted: the page says 'they [SST] can provide their users with better visibility' (a future plan); the claim says 'Pulumi Insights provides better visibility' (a product feature)
verdicts.intuition_flag: The link may not fit: Insights is sold for resource search and analytics, not deployment monitoring or observability, so pointing 'better visibility into the deployment process' at the Insights page could mislead readers.

verdicts.text: Pulumi Crosswalk for AWS simplifies "day one" tasks, as described in the AWS guide at /docs/iac/guides/clouds/aws/.
verdicts.evidence: The linked AWS guide no longer mentions "Crosswalk" or "day one". The old /docs/reference/crosswalk/aws/ and /docs/guides/crosswalk/ URLs now just redirect to it, and it opens: "This section contains guides for working with AWS services using Pulumi." The idea behind the claim still holds, since providers.md says AWSx "packages common AWS patterns into opinionated, reusable constructs", but the line credits the guide with a description it doesn't give, and the Crosswalk name looks outdated.
verdicts.framing_note: shifted — the guide describes AWS guides and AWSx component libraries; the claim says it describes how "Pulumi Crosswalk for AWS simplifies 'day one' tasks"
verdicts.intuition_flag: Old Crosswalk wording in a blog CTA; the target page has dropped the Crosswalk name (the Crosswalk URLs now redirect to it), so the link text may need updating to say AWSx or the AWS guides.

verdicts.text: An on-demand Pulumi workshop titled "Getting Started with Infrastructure as Code on AWS" exists at https://www.pulumi.com/resources/getting-started-with-iac-pulumi-aws/.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) A Pulumi workshop called "Getting Started with Infrastructure as Code on AWS" does exist. Its indexed page describes it this way: "This workshop is designed to help new users become familiar with the core concepts needed to effectively deploy resources on AWS using Pulumi." However, search only returned it under /events/getting-started-with-iac-pulumi-aws/, not the cited /resources/ path. I couldn't confirm that the /resources/ URL resolves or redirects, or that the workshop is on-demand.
verdicts.framing_note: The title matches, but the URL doesn't: the page is indexed at /events/..., while the claim cites /resources/... "On-demand" isn't confirmed either.
verdicts.intuition_flag: The /resources/ path may be an old URL. Check whether content/events/getting-started-with-iac-pulumi-aws has an alias for /resources/..., or whether the link will 404.

verdicts.text: Pulumi offers upcoming Platform Engineering or DevOps workshops listed at https://www.pulumi.com/resources/#upcoming.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) Web search confirms that Pulumi runs Platform Engineering / DevOps workshops. But the current events listing is at pulumi.com/events/ ("Pulumi Events & Workshops"), and no result showed that /resources/ or its #upcoming anchor still exists or still lists upcoming workshops.
verdicts.source: WebSearch ran query "Pulumi upcoming workshops platform engineering"; https://www.pulumi.com/events/
verdicts.intuition_flag: The link /resources/#upcoming may be out of date; upcoming events now seem to be listed at /events/. Check for a redirect or anchor in the repo (layouts/, content/resources/).

verdicts.text: The Pulumi Cloud signup page is at https://app.pulumi.com/signup.
verdicts.evidence: L180 links "[try Pulumi](https://app.pulumi.com/signup)". Other pages link to the same URL, e.g. confirmation/workshop.md uses href="https://app.pulumi.com/signup", and scripts/redirects/signup-redirects.txt sends "signup/index.html|https://app.pulumi.com/signup".

verdicts.text: A blog post exists at /blog/sst-built-on-pulumi/ titled "SST Runs on the Pulumi Engine: What It Means to Build on Pulumi", and it covers the engine mechanics behind SST's migration from CDK to Pulumi.
verdicts.evidence: pulumi/docs PR #21651 adds "content/blog/sst-built-on-pulumi/index.md: 'SST Runs on the Pulumi Engine: What It Means to Build on Pulumi.'" It says the post covers "what 'built on the Pulumi engine' means mechanically", with SST as the lead example. The title and path match. I could not confirm that the post is merged or live.
verdicts.framing_note: The companion PR says the new post is about engine mechanics, with "SST is the lead example, not the subject"; the migration story stays in the 2024 post. The claim's "engine mechanics behind SST's migration" is a slightly loose summary but fits that scope.
verdicts.intuition_flag: The target post comes from a separate PR (#21651); check that it merges before or with this cross-link, or the link will 404.

verdicts.text: SST (Serverless Stack) is a framework that makes building modern full-stack applications on your infrastructure easy.
verdicts.evidence: SST's official docs describe it this way: "SST is a framework that makes it easy to build modern full-stack applications on your own infrastructure." The claim is a close paraphrase of that sentence.
verdicts.framing_note: The claim says 'on your infrastructure' where the source says 'on your own infrastructure'. This is only a wording change and the meaning is the same.

verdicts.text: In SST Ion, constructs (components) are deployed using Pulumi instead of CDK and CloudFormation.
verdicts.evidence: SST's own "Moving away from CDK" post says: "The constructs (or components) are defined using Terraform providers and deployed using Pulumi; as opposed to CDK and CloudFormation (CFN)." The SST v3 post backs this up: Ion is a deployment engine that uses "Pulumi and Terraform, as opposed to CDK and CloudFormation."
verdicts.framing_note: The source says components are "defined using Terraform providers and deployed using Pulumi". The claim leaves out the Terraform-provider part but gets the deployment part right.

verdicts.text: Ion is the code name for a new engine for deploying SST applications, in which constructs/components are deployed using Pulumi instead of CDK and CloudFormation.
verdicts.evidence: SST's own announcement says: "Ion is a code name for a new engine for deploying SST applications." It adds that components are "defined using Terraform providers and deployed using Pulumi; as opposed to CDK and CloudFormation (CFN)." SST's v3 post confirms this and says Ion shipped as SST v3.
verdicts.framing_note: The source says components are 'defined using Terraform providers and deployed using Pulumi; as opposed to CDK and CloudFormation'. The claim leaves out the Terraform-providers part, but the source still fully supports the deployment statement.
verdicts.intuition_flag: The blog's wording ('Once Ion is stable, it will be released as SST v3') is out of date. Ion shipped as SST v3 in August 2024, so the post may want a tense update.

verdicts.text: Once Ion is stable, it will be released as SST v3 (temporal framing: Ion is described as not yet stable).
verdicts.evidence: This line comes from SST's January 2024 post ("Once Ion is stable, it'll be released as SST v3"), but it is now out of date. SST's August 20, 2024 post says "Ion is now officially being released as SST v3," so describing Ion as not yet stable is wrong as of 2026.
verdicts.framing_note: shifted — a 2024 future-tense plan ('will be released as SST v3') is still stated as pending, but it was done in Aug 2024. Fix: past tense ('Ion was released as SST v3 in August 2024') or label it as a quote from SST's Jan 2024 post.

verdicts.text: In SST's deploy chain: SST resolves components from `sst.config.ts` and compiles them into Pulumi resource declarations; the Pulumi engine diffs desired vs. actual state, builds a dependency graph, and orders operations; Terraform-bridged providers (via Pulumi's Terraform bridge) translate each resource into cloud API calls; state is written to an S3 bucket in the user's AWS account.
verdicts.evidence: SST's source (pkg/project/provider/aws.go, decoded) has a bootstrap step, "Step: create the bootstrap bucket", which runs `stateName := fmt.Sprintf("sst-state-%v", rand)` under the user's own AWS credentials and records `State string json:"state"`. It also defines `ErrBucketMissing = errors.New("sst state bucket missing")`, which confirms state lives in an S3 bucket in the user's account. The engine steps (diff desired vs. actual state, build a dependency graph, order operations) and the Terraform-bridged providers such as pulumi-aws match how Pulumi is documented to work.
verdicts.framing_note: State goes to S3 only when the app's home is AWS; SST also supports Cloudflare as a home, which uses a different state backend. Not every SST provider is Terraform-bridged, but the main ones (AWS, Cloudflare) are.

verdicts.text: SST's dependency on the Pulumi engine has not changed despite the team's broadened attention to opencode, and SST's release cadence has not changed.

verdicts.text: `sst deploy` reads your `sst.config.ts`, resolves SST's own components, and compiles them into Pulumi resource declarations (a step handled by SST rather than the Pulumi engine).

That confirms SST's own component layer turns config into Pulumi resource registrations, which the engine then takes over. One wording caveat: "compile" is loose. The components run as a Pulumi program and register resources at runtime rather than being compiled.
verdicts.intuition_flag: "Compiles into Pulumi resource declarations" suggests a code-generation step. In practice SST components are Pulumi ComponentResources that register resources when the program runs.

verdicts.text: The Pulumi engine diffs desired versus actual state, builds a dependency graph, and orders operations in an SST deployment.
verdicts.evidence: The Pulumi docs say "The deployment engine computes the set of operations needed to drive the current state of your infrastructure into the desired state expressed by your program." The engine source includes pkg/resource/deploy/step_generator.go, which plans and orders steps using resource dependencies. The SST quotes elsewhere in the post back up that SST embeds this engine.
verdicts.intuition_flag: Small imprecision: by default Pulumi diffs against the last recorded state in the state file, not live cloud state (that needs `pulumi refresh`), and providers compute the per-resource diffs.

verdicts.text: AWS alone exposes hundreds of resource types, each with its own create, update, and delete semantics.

verdicts.text: Pulumi's engine does not require a Pulumi account, a network call to Pulumi Cloud, or any Pulumi-hosted service to run.

That means the engine can run without a Pulumi account or Pulumi Cloud. The CLI does make some optional calls by default, such as update checks and plugin downloads, but these aren't required.
verdicts.intuition_flag: "Any Pulumi-hosted service" is absolute. By default the CLI may contact Pulumi-hosted endpoints (the update check, plugin downloads from get.pulumi.com). These can be avoided, so they aren't required, but the wording is strong.

verdicts.text: Pulumi's Automation API works by embedding the Pulumi engine for teams embedding Pulumi programs inside their own tools, in the same embedding manner SST does.

verdicts.text: - **SST users are not Pulumi Cloud customers.** SST's state lives in your own S3 bucket, not in Pulumi's hosted service, and SST doesn't require a Pulumi account to work.
verdicts.evidence: SST's state docs (base64-decoded) say: "The state is generated locally but is backed up to your provider using: A **bucket** to store the state, typically named `sst-state-<hash>`", and "Currently `aws` and `cloudflare` are supported." So state sits in your own cloud bucket, not in Pulumi Cloud. The doc never says outright that no Pulumi account is needed; I inferred that from this self-hosted state design.
verdicts.framing_note: The claim says an S3 bucket. SST supports both an AWS home (S3) and a Cloudflare home (R2), so "S3" is only the AWS case. Either way, state is in the user's own bucket.

verdicts.text: Most SST users never write a line of Pulumi code and work entirely in SST's component model; SST keeps its own abstractions and API.
verdicts.evidence: This is an unsourced claim about how a third party's users behave. Nothing in pulumi/* or the local repo measures what share of SST users write Pulumi code. The post's own quoted source (Blandin) says only that SST "lets users write Pulumi code in addition to using SST's constructs", which supports "SST keeps its own abstractions" but not "most users never write Pulumi code".
verdicts.source: repo:content/blog/sst-built-on-pulumi/index.md L61, L101 (context only; no independent source found)
verdicts.intuition_flag: "Most SST users never write a line of Pulumi code" is stated as fact with no data behind it. Consider softening it (e.g., "many SST apps never need to") or adding a source.

verdicts.text: Because SST's components compile to Pulumi resources, users can define resources directly in Pulumi inside an SST app for anything lacking a dedicated SST construct, and deploy them as part of the same app.
verdicts.evidence: SST's own providers docs say "SST is built on Pulumi/Terraform and supports 150+ providers" and "The provider packages come with components that you can use in your app." They show `new aws.s3.BucketV2(...)` declared right next to `new sst.aws.Function(...)` in sst.config.ts, and add that SST's built-in components are "higher level components" on top of the provider components.
verdicts.framing_note: SST's docs show raw Pulumi provider resources and SST components declared in the same sst.config.ts. The claim's reason, that SST components 'compile to Pulumi resources', is the blog's own paraphrase of 'built on Pulumi'.

verdicts.text: The `sst` npm package gets roughly 796,000 downloads a week (796,291 downloads for the week of September 5-11, 2026, per the npm downloads API).
verdicts.evidence: Wrong target: the claim credits the npm downloads API, but the pre-fetched page is opencode.ai. That page only covers OpenCode ("over 208,000 GitHub stars... used and trusted by over 16M developers every month") and says nothing about weekly downloads of the `sst` npm package.
verdicts.framing_note: The claim names the npm downloads API (api.npmjs.org/downloads/point/...), but the fetched URL is opencode.ai, so I didn't run the framing check against it.
verdicts.intuition_flag: A precise weekly count for September 5-11, 2026 should be checked against api.npmjs.org/downloads/point/2026-09-05:2026-09-11/sst. The date may also be in the future or a typo.

verdicts.text: opencode (anomalyco/opencode) has grown quickly since launch and now has a larger GitHub following (star count) than SST itself, as observed September 2026.
verdicts.evidence: The cited page returned HTTP 200, but the pre-fetched body cuts off after the title ("GitHub - anomalyco/opencode: The open source coding agent. · GitHub"). It shows no star count for opencode or SST, so the comparison can't be checked from it.
verdicts.framing_note: The page loaded but its fetched content doesn't include star counts. The claim's comparison with SST also needs the sst/sst repo page, which wasn't cited.
verdicts.intuition_flag: Star counts change over time. The claim is pinned to "September 2026", and the fetched page gives no way to confirm that timestamp. A reviewer should compare the live star counts of both repos.

verdicts.text: SST is not being abandoned; releases and download numbers indicate continued activity.
verdicts.evidence: The GitHub release list shows ongoing SST releases: "v4.17.1 Latest 2026-07-12", v4.17.0 (2026-06-26), v4.16.0 (2026-06-24) and v4.15.x (2026-05-29). That supports "continued activity". I didn't check the npm figure of about 796K weekly downloads here.
verdicts.framing_note: "Not being abandoned" is an interpretation. The release history backs it, but the download count wasn't independently confirmed.

verdicts.text: Anyone who runs SST is already running Pulumi's engine, whether or not they have written any Pulumi code.
verdicts.evidence: SST's CLI go.mod (sst/sst, now anomalyco/sst, branch dev) requires `github.com/pulumi/pulumi/pkg/v3 v3.215.0` and `github.com/pulumi/pulumi/sdk/v3 v3.215.0`, so the Pulumi engine is built into the SST CLI and `sst deploy` runs on it even if the user never writes Pulumi code. One caveat: this only holds for SST v3. SST v2 and earlier ran on CDK, though the post says v3 has been the only supported version since mid-2024.
verdicts.intuition_flag: "Anyone who runs SST" leaves out legacy SST v2 (CDK-based) users, so the sentence could say "SST v3" to be exact.

verdicts.text: Yes. Since SST v3 (the Ion rewrite, shipped mid-2024), `sst deploy` runs through an embedded Pulumi engine that calls Terraform-bridged providers to make the underlying cloud API calls, replacing SST's earlier architecture on AWS CDK and CloudFormation.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) SST's own SST v3 announcement (dated August 20, 2024) says "Ion is now officially being released as SST v3" and that "SST was built on AWS CDK and CloudFormation." It also describes the new engine as one that "would use Pulumi and Terraform, as opposed to CDK and CloudFormation." SST's earlier post adds that components are "defined using Terraform providers and deployed using Pulumi."
verdicts.framing_note: An August 2024 release counts as "mid-2024" under a loose reading. The phrase "embedded Pulumi engine" goes a little past the sources' wording ("deployed using Pulumi"), but it fits how SST works.

verdicts.text: SST's components are defined using Terraform providers that are bridged through the Pulumi engine; SST does not invoke the Terraform CLI or write Terraform state.
verdicts.evidence: SST's docs say "SST uses Pulumi behind the scenes for the providers and the deployment engine. And Terraform's providers are bridged through Pulumi." The SST v3 post says state "is stored locally and backed up to S3 in your AWS account", which is Pulumi's state model, not Terraform state. No source says outright that SST never invokes the Terraform CLI, but that follows from the architecture: the bridge connects the Pulumi engine straight to the Terraform provider over RPC.
verdicts.framing_note: SST says 'Terraform's providers are bridged through Pulumi' and Pulumi is 'the deployment engine'. The claim's added part (no Terraform CLI, no Terraform state) is inferred from that, not stated word for word. 'Components are defined using Terraform providers' is a loose paraphrase of 'SST uses Pulumi providers, which are bridged from Terraform'.

verdicts.text: Yes. SST shipped v4.17.1 in July 2026 and the `sst` package continues to see roughly 796,000 weekly downloads on npm. The team's public attention has broadened to include opencode, an open source AI coding agent, but that hasn't changed SST's release cadence or its dependency on the Pulumi engine.
verdicts.evidence: The version and date check out: the GitHub release page shows v4.17.1 as "thdxr released this · 12 Jul 20:18 · v4.17.1", and the v4.17.0 assets are dated 2026-06-26, so it's July 2026. I couldn't confirm the ~796,000 weekly downloads figure. The only public number I found was npmtrends showing "sst 4.13.1 which has 467,885 weekly downloads", which is an older snapshot. I didn't check the opencode and release-cadence parts.
verdicts.source: https://github.com/anomalyco/sst/releases/tag/v4.17.1; https://npmtrends.com/create-serverless-stack-vs-sst; WebSearch ran query "npmtrends sst weekly downloads 4.17.1"
verdicts.intuition_flag: Weekly download counts change all the time. The claimed 796k is about 1.7x the older 468k npmtrends figure, so check it against api.npmjs.org/downloads/point/last-week/sst before publishing.

verdicts.text: The docs page /docs/iac/guides/basics/how-pulumi-works/ exists and explains the engine mechanics.
verdicts.evidence: I found the page at content/docs/iac/guides/basics/how-pulumi-works.md, titled "How Pulumi IaC Works", which puts it at /docs/iac/guides/basics/how-pulumi-works/. It explains how the engine works: "Three main components work together when you run `pulumi up`: a language host, a deployment engine, and resource providers". It also walks through resource registration, comparing desired state with current state, and deciding the order to create and delete resources.

verdicts.text: The blog post /blog/any-terraform-provider/ is titled "Introducing: Support For Using Any Terraform Provider with Pulumi" and covers the bridge SST and others build on.
verdicts.evidence: The page at /blog/any-terraform-provider/ is titled "Introducing: Support For Using Any Terraform Provider with Pulumi | Pulumi Blog". It says Pulumi is "introducing support for using any Terraform or OpenTofu provider from within your Pulumi programs," which runs on the Terraform bridge / parameterized-provider technology.
verdicts.framing_note: The title matches exactly. "Covers the bridge SST and others build on" is a loose editorial description. The post is about the Any Terraform Provider feature, which is built on the Terraform bridge, and it does not mention SST.

verdicts.text: The Automation API docs page shows how other tools embed Pulumi the same way SST does.
verdicts.evidence: The link target resolves: content/docs/iac/concepts/automation-api.md serves /docs/iac/concepts/automation-api/. Under its use cases it lists "Building higher-level tools, such as custom CLIs over Pulumi" and "Exposing Pulumi behind a REST or gRPC API", which is the embedding pattern the claim describes.
verdicts.framing_note: The page describes the general pattern ("building higher-level tools") but doesn't name other tools. So "shows how other tools embed Pulumi" is a loose paraphrase of the page's intent, not something the page literally shows.

verdicts.text: [^npm-downloads]: [npm download stats for `sst`](https://api.npmjs.org/downloads/point/last-week/sst), 796,291 downloads for the week of September 5-11, 2026.
verdicts.evidence: The cited endpoint gives a rolling last-7-days count. When fetched, it returned `{"downloads":1334575,"start":"2026-09-21","end":"2026-09-27","package":"sst"}`, which covers a different week from the claimed September 5-11, 2026. So it can neither confirm nor contradict the 796,291 figure.
verdicts.framing_note: The source's rolling 'last-week' window (Sep 21-27, 1,334,575) doesn't match the claim's fixed 'week of September 5-11' (796,291). A fixed-date endpoint such as /downloads/point/2026-09-05:2026-09-11/sst would pin the figure down.
verdicts.intuition_flag: This footnote points to a rolling 'last-week' URL to back a fixed-date number, so the link will never show the stated value. Change it to a date-range endpoint. Also, the latest week (~1.33M) is well above the cited 796K, so the number may be stale.
